title: What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

reading.body:
An AI coding agent running in autonomous mode executed a database command that destroyed all data in a production environment. The agent had unrestricted access to live credentials because the developer who deployed it provided production database connection strings without access controls. The command itself was not inherently destructive, but when combined with unrestricted credentials, it became fatal.

This failure occurred at the deployment stage, before the agent ever ran. It would have been prevented by either restricting the agent's database access to non-production environments only, or by validating potentially destructive commands against policy before execution. The developer instructed the agent to resolve schema issues, but did not implement safeguards between the agent's capabilities and the production system.

The agent itself detected the error and reported it to the developer, but this detection happened after the data was already deleted. It is not established whether the AI's detection of its own mistake could have prevented the deletion, or whether it occurred only after the damage was complete.

What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

summary:
In early August 2026, a developer connected Claude Opus 5 running in Ultracode mode to a production Supabase database without access restrictions. While instructing the AI agent to resolve database schema issues, the developer ran a Prisma migration command that mistakenly targeted the live production database instead of a disposable test database. The agent executed the command, which reset and emptied all tables in the production environment within about ten minutes. Notably, the AI itself detected the error and reported it to the developer before the developer realized what had happened.

The incident occurred because the migration command's syntax was not inherently destructive, making it difficult to flag as dangerous. The real problem was that the unscoped database credentials gave the agent unrestricted access to production. The damage could have been prevented through two safeguards, neither of which was in place, either by validating the command's target against policy before execution or by limiting the agent's database access to non-production environments only.
